title: Knapsack interdiction, optimum
description: The bilevel knapsack as an optimisation problem: the smallest profit the leader can hold the follower to, and every set of locked items that achieves it. The abstraction proposes locked items with a claimed value, smallest claim first; the follower's best packing refutes a claim and is grounded as a rule that later claims have to cover. The first candidate that survives has the optimal value (25); a second program part then forbids larger claims, and the loop lists the other optimal choices.

fragments.name: shared
fragments.description: The items. Added to every solver.
fragments.text:
% The instance (its facts) is in the Instances tab.
% top(T): no packing is worth more than T.
top(T) :- T = #sum { P,I : item(I,_,_,P) }.

fragments.name: abstraction
fragments.description: Proposes candidates (solver A): locked items and a claimed value, smallest claim first.
fragments.text:
% A candidate: locked items within the budget ...
{ lock(I) : item(I,_,_,_) }.
:- #sum { C,I : lock(I), item(I,C,_,_) } > budget.
% ... and a claim: the follower cannot get more than V. Small claims are preferred.
1 { value(V) : V = 0..T } 1 :- top(T).
#minimize { V : value(V) }.
#show lock/1.
#show value/1.

fragments.name: refine
fragments.description: Two parts: refine(k) per counterexample packing, cap(k) once the optimum is known.
fragments.text:
#program refine(k).
% cex(k,pack(I)): the k-th counterexample packs item I. Its profit:
profit(k,P) :- P = #sum { Q,I : cex(k,pack(I)), item(I,_,_,Q) }.
% The claim has to cover this profit unless one of the packed items is locked.
hit(k) :- cex(k,pack(I)), lock(I).
:- not hit(k), profit(k,P), value(V), V < P.

#program cap(k).
% best(k,value(B)): the optimal value B is known. No larger claim is of interest.
:- best(k,value(B)), value(V), V > B.

fragments.name: glue
fragments.description: The interface atoms: the locked items and the claim.

fragments.name: check
fragments.description: Looks for a packing of the remaining items worth more than the claim (solver C).
fragments.text:
% A counterexample: the follower packs items that are not locked, within the capacity,
% and gets more than the claimed value.
{ pack(I) : item(I,_,_,_) }.
:- pack(I), lock(I).
:- #sum { W,I : pack(I), item(I,_,W,_) } > capacity.
:- value(V), #sum { P,I : pack(I), item(I,_,_,P) } <= V.
% With 'optimal' the follower's best packing comes back (the strongest counterexample).
#minimize { -P,I : pack(I), item(I,_,_,P) }.
#show pack/1.

loop.text:
solver A = shared + abstraction + refine
solver C = shared + check
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue

# An optimisation loop. A.solve(optimal) returns locked items with the smallest claim
# that is still possible; C.solve(..., optimal) answers with the follower's best
# packing if it beats the claim. The packing is grounded into A (part refine): later
# claims have to cover it. The first candidate that survives the check has the optimal
# value. The part cap then forbids larger claims, so the loop goes on to list the
# other optimal choices and ends when A has no candidate left.
capped = false
loop:
    M = A.solve(optimal)
    if not M: stop
    X = C.solve(assume G(M), optimal)
    if X:
        A.expand(refine, cex = X.atoms(pack/1))
    else:
        accept M
        A.add(G.block(M))
        if not capped:
            A.expand(cap, best = M.atoms(value/1))
            capped = true

library.summary: Bilevel knapsack optimisation: an optimal abstraction gives lower bounds, the follower's best replies are grounded as rules, and a second part caps the claims (optimum 25, 2 solutions).
